crime.value: Shooting death of Lucas Pitman (a law enforcement officer) by his wife Lucretia with a Winchester .30-caliber rifle; central question: was this self-defense or murder, and what led to the act?
crime.quote: Two bullets. For the first was not enough to stop him.

victim.value: Lucas Pitman, a deputy sheriff with a violent, controlling temperament who stalks, manipulates, and physically threatens his young wife; 'killable' due to his abusive behavior and implied history of violence toward women
victim.quote: A man's fingers closing around my throat. There is nothing so terrible as strangulation.

closed_world.value: The Pitman-Rayburn household in Au Sable Forks, a remote Adirondack region where 'everyone is acquainted with everyone else since grade school'; a rural country house isolated by geography and social insularity
closed_world.quote: in Au Sable Forks, which is the center and circumference of my world

culprit_and_motive.value: Lucretia Pitman (the narrator) kills her husband in an act of self-defense or desperation; motive is fear of imminent physical harm, strangulation, and escape from an abusive, controlling marriage
culprit_and_motive.quote: It was to keep him from hurting me. It was to keep him at a distance.

resolution.value: Everett Rayburn (Lucretia's father) arrives and orchestrates the narrative; they call 911 and his lawyer; Lucretia is instructed to tell the truth of self-defense, restoring legal and familial order through paternal intervention
resolution.quote: 'Just tell the truth, Lucretia.' Which is what I will do, so help me God.

investigator.value: Lucretia Pitman herself—the narrator and protagonist—experiences the mystery as victim, suspect, and unreliable witness to her own act; her consciousness frames the entire investigation
investigator.quote: I am waiting for him, hiding. I think that I am starkly sober as a creature that has been skinned alive

suspect_architecture.value: Single-suspect domestic violence narrative: husband Pitman (law enforcement officer, history of strangulation threats, armed, controlling) as sole perpetrator; no competing suspects. Narrator Lucretia is both victim and killer. Cousin Andrea peripherally implicated via suggested prior intimacy with Pitman, but functions as witness only.
suspect_architecture.quote: There has been this shivery thing between her and Pitman dating back to before Pitman and I were married.

red_herring.value: The anonymous obscene phone caller is presented as a threatening stranger (UNAVAILABLE, sexually menacing), misdirecting both Lucretia and the reader toward an external threat; ultimately the terror driving the shooting is Pitman's domestic violence, not the caller. Also, Lucretia's drunken state is foregrounded to suggest unreliable agency, potentially misdirecting judgment of premeditation.
red_herring.quote: UNAVAILABLE could be anyone. Like seeing on your doorstep a hulking individual wearing a paper bag over his head, or a ski mask.

clue_fairness.value: Key clues are embedded in the narrator's retrospective account and available to the reader simultaneously: Pitman's prior strangulation games on Hunter Road, the loaded rifle's location described earlier, the murder/suicide of Amos Burdock (strangulation), and Pitman arriving home early. Phone records timestamped at 1:14 A.M. are disclosed to the reader before any official investigation.
clue_fairness.quote: I called home at 1:14 A.M. Not 911. Phone records will show.

social_world.value: Rural Adirondack class hierarchy: wealthy contractor Rayburns versus low-status Pitman clan ('feared and scorned in about equal measure'); law enforcement as a masculinist power structure shielding Pitman from accountability; patriarchal family authority (father disowning daughter); institutional impunity for police use of force ('never been reprimanded for excessive force').
social_world.quote: The Pitmans and their numerous kin were not generally respected. They were feared and scorned in about equal measure.

alibi.value: No formal alibi construction for Pitman; instead, Lucretia's self-defense claim functions as the alibi-equivalent narrative she must construct for authorities. Daddy coaches her: 'What you will say, Lucretia, is…' and 'Just tell the truth'—framing the shooting as self-defense. Pitman's early return home (1 A.M. vs. usual 2:50 A.M.) is a temporal clue undermining any alibi for his absence.
alibi.quote: It's a bad sign, Pitman arrives home early… tonight his headlights swing into the driveway at just 1 A.M. So I know.

reveal_mechanic.value: The solution is demonstrated through accumulation of embodied physical detail rather than deductive reasoning: two bullet casings (first shot insufficient), the rifle found on the floor, Daddy's wordless inspection of the body, and Lucretia's dissociated 'skinned-alive' state. The reveal is psychological and forensic simultaneously—two bullets proving the killing was effortful, not cold execution.
reveal_mechanic.quote: Two bullets. For the first was not enough to stop him.

media_and_audience.value: Local newspaper coverage of the Burdock murder/suicide frames domestic homicide as a 'those people' spectacle for respectable classes; Lucretia's mother enacts this distancing ('Such an ugly story! Those people'). The narrative anticipates a public/legal audience—phone records, 911 call, Daddy's lawyer—suggesting the crime will be packaged as self-defense for institutional consumption.
media_and_audience.quote: 'Such an ugly story! Those people.' My mother spoke with repugnance, disdain. Those people referred to people who got themselves killed.

investigator_wound.value: There is no external investigator; Lucretia herself is the only investigative consciousness, and her wound is total: six years of coercive control, sexual surveillance, strangulation threats, and her father's disownment have destroyed her capacity for self-protective action until the final moment. Her vulnerability is her love for Pitman coexisting with terror of him—'I love him! Want him to forgive me.'
investigator_wound.quote: I love him! Want him to forgive me. I will beg him I didn't mean it, I was only pretending.
